--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Risk Management ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Distinguish** risk from uncertainty, and threats from opportunities. 2. **Classify** a risk and write a well-formed risk statement. 3. **Run** a qualitative analysis with a probability--impact matrix. 4. **Compute** expected monetary value (EMV) and solve a simple decision tree. 5. **Select** a response strategy: accept, minimize, share, transfer, or reserve. 6. **Size** a contingency reserve and distinguish task contingency from managerial contingency. 7. **Explain** how FMEA supports project risk management.
Before we begin: name one thing that could sink the RC-vehicle project Now: how likely is it, and how bad would it be? You just did qualitative risk analysis. The rest of this chapter makes it systematic.
## Introduction: the known unknowns The RC-vehicle brief is a risk register waiting to be written. One candidate motor supplier is **unproven** and its staff are **negotiating a first labour contract**. The carbon-fibre supplier is **mid-restructuring** after a foreign acquisition. Choosing a **new assembly line** brings a **learning curve**. None of these is a certainty --- but each is *identifiable*, and that is exactly what makes it a **risk** rather than an uncertainty. > **Risk** = the probability or threat of loss, injury, or any negative > occurrence caused by internal or external vulnerabilities, that **can be > reduced by preemptive action**. > > An **uncertainty** is when *neither* the probability *nor* the mode of > occurrence is known. If you do not know about it, you cannot act on it. The core equation: $$\text{Risk} = \text{Probability of event} \times \text{Impact of event}$$ Probability is usually a percentage; impact is dollars or schedule delay. **Risk and opportunity are mirror images** --- an opportunity is an unforeseen event with a *positive* outcome, handled with the same tools for the opposite end. ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** Aircraft makers such as Bombardier **minimize** part risk by forcing every significant supplier into direct contact with their quality department and auditing their processes. The European Space Agency and Airbus **share** the risk of a new airframe across nations because no one country can carry it. A fixed-price defense contract **transfers** budget-overrun risk to the vendor. :::
## The four-stage process 1. **Risk identification** --- determine the specific risk factors that can reasonably be expected to affect the project. 2. **Analysis of probability and consequences** --- how likely, and how bad. 3. **Risk mitigation strategies** --- steps to reduce the impact of the risks judged threatening enough to act on. 4. **Control and documentation** --- track the risks and build a **knowledge base** for future projects from the lessons learned. ## Risk identification and classification Sort each identified risk into a class. A common (not exhaustive) list: - **Financial** --- material price moves, currency, budget cuts - **Technology** --- unproven design or process - **Resources** --- key people, equipment availability - **Schedule** --- dependency slips, long lead times - **Weather**, **Political**, **Environmental** Techniques: structured **brainstorming**, **interviewing** to get optimistic / most-likely / pessimistic views of an event, **probability distributions** to represent uncertain outcomes, and **expert judgment** to validate. ## Qualitative analysis: the probability--impact matrix Plot each risk by **likelihood** (x-axis) and **impact** (y-axis). The top-right is **red** (mitigation planned in advance), the middle band **yellow** (team decides whether to plan), the bottom-left **green** (just stay aware). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- expand.grid(prob = 1:5, impact = 1:5) grid$score <- grid$prob * grid$impact grid$zone <- cut(grid$score, c(0, 6, 12, 25), labels = c("Green", "Yellow", "Red")) risks <- data.frame( risk = c("Unproven supplier can't deliver", "Carbon-fibre plant disruption", "New line learning curve overruns", "Labour action at supplier", "Steel price spike", "Minor drawing errors"), prob = c(3, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4), impact = c(5, 4, 3, 5, 2, 1) ) ggplot(grid, aes(prob, impact)) + geom_tile(aes(fill = zone), color = "white", linewidth = 1) + scale_fill_manual(values = c(Green = "#A9DFBF", Yellow = "#F9E79F", Red = "#F5B7B1"), name = "Zone") + geom_point(data = risks, aes(prob, impact), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3, color = "#1B4F72") + geom_text(data = risks, aes(prob, impact, label = risk), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.7 * diagram_text_scale, vjust = -1, hjust = 0.5) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = c("Very low", "Low", "Medium", "High", "Very high")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = c("Negligible", "Minor", "Moderate", "Major", "Severe")) + labs(title = "Probability x Impact", x = "Probability", y = "Impact") + theme_minimal() + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 14 * diagram_text_scale, face = "bold"), axis.title = element_text(size = 11 * diagram_text_scale), axis.text = element_text(size = 9.5 * diagram_text_scale) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Probability-impact matrix for the RC-vehicle project. Red-zone risks (unproven supplier failure, carbon-fibre disruption) get a written mitigation plan before anything goes wrong.](07-Risk-Management_files/figure-html/fig-pi-matrix-07-1.png){#fig-pi-matrix-07 fig-align='center' width=912} ::: ::: ## Quantitative analysis Tools: **sensitivity analysis** (which risks move the outcome most), **expected monetary value** (the probability-weighted average outcome), **decision trees** (lay out choices and chance events), and **Monte Carlo** simulation (run the network thousands of times with sampled durations/costs). ### Worked Example 1: EMV of a single risk The "new assembly line learning curve" risk: a **40 %** chance it adds **\$120 000** of rework and overtime; otherwise \$0. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_occurs <- 0.40 impact <- 120000 emv <- p_occurs * impact + (1 - p_occurs) * 0 cat(sprintf("EMV of this risk: 0.40 x $%s = $%s\n", format(impact, big.mark = " "), format(emv, big.mark = " "))) cat("This is the amount you would budget in a risk reserve to 'cover' this one risk on average.\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EMV of this risk: 0.40 x $120 000 = $48 000 This is the amount you would budget in a risk reserve to 'cover' this one risk on average. ``` ::: ::: ### Try it yourself: decision tree --- buy the copper now or later? You need **750 lb of copper** for the RC-vehicle wiring harness tooling. Buy it **now** and pay **\$100** storage, or buy it **later** at the summer price --- which is **\$5.58/lb with 90 % probability**, or **\$4.50/lb with 10 % probability**. ```{webr-r} #| label: decision-tree-07 lb <- 750 storage <- 100 # Branch: buy now (price locked, pay storage) buy_now <- 5.58 * lb + storage # Branch: buy later (two chance outcomes) p_high <- 0.90; price_high <- 5.58 p_low <- 0.10; price_low <- 4.50 buy_later <- p_high * (price_high * lb) + p_low * (price_low * lb) cat(sprintf("EMV, buy now : $%.2f\n", buy_now)) cat(sprintf("EMV, buy later: 0.90 x $%.2f + 0.10 x $%.2f = $%.2f\n", price_high * lb, price_low * lb, buy_later)) cat(sprintf("\nChoose: %s (saves $%.2f on average)\n", ifelse(buy_later < buy_now, "BUY LATER", "BUY NOW"), abs(buy_now - buy_later))) ```
What would flip the decision? Raise the probability of the low summer price, widen the price gap, or cut the storage cost toward zero and "buy later" wins by more. Push storage cost up (a bonded warehouse, insurance, spoilage) or make the high price nearly certain and "buy now" wins. A decision tree makes the tipping point explicit instead of leaving it to gut feel.
## Response strategies | Strategy | What it means | Example on our project | |---|---|---| | **Accept** | The risk is minor or unlikely enough to live with | Small drawing errors --- caught in review, low cost | | **Minimize** | Reduce probability or impact | Audit the unproven supplier; put their staff in contact with your quality team | | **Share** | Split the risk (and reward) with a partner | Co-develop the new control system with the supplier under a shared-savings deal | | **Transfer** | Shift the risk to another party | Fixed-price contract (vendor eats overruns); **liquidated damages** for non-performance | | **Contingency reserve** | Set aside funds/time for the risk if it hits | 10--15 % reserve against the carbon-fibre and learning-curve risks | | **Other** | Anything else fit for the situation | Dual-source the motor; pre-qualify a backup | For **opportunities**, the mirror strategies are **exploit, share, enhance,** and **accept**. ## Contingency reserves Two kinds: - **Task (project) contingency** --- offsets overruns on individual tasks/work packages. **Managed by the project manager.** As work completes, reserve for finished tasks is released and cannot be reused. - **Managerial contingency** --- a project-level buffer for scope changes forced by the customer, "acts of God," and other unforeseeable events. **Managed by senior management, not the PM.** In construction it is common to set aside **10--15 %** of the price. Other industries resist it --- the customer may read a visible reserve as a sign of poor planning. ### Try it yourself: does the mitigation pay for itself? ```{webr-r} #| label: mitigation-value-07 # Risk: unproven supplier fails to deliver on time. p_fail_no_action <- 0.35 impact_if_fail <- 260000 # expedite alternative source + line downtime # Mitigation: pre-qualify a backup supplier now. mitigation_cost <- 22000 p_fail_with_action <- 0.10 # backup ready -> failure much less damaging impact_with_action <- 90000 # switch to backup, smaller hit emv_before <- p_fail_no_action * impact_if_fail emv_after <- mitigation_cost + p_fail_with_action * impact_with_action cat(sprintf("EMV, do nothing : $%s\n", format(round(emv_before), big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("EMV, pre-qualify backup : $%s (incl. $%s spent now)\n", format(round(emv_after), big.mark = " "), format(mitigation_cost, big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("\nExpected saving from acting: $%s\n", format(round(emv_before - emv_after), big.mark = " "))) ``` ## FMEA as a risk tool **Failure Mode and Effects Analysis** is often the first step of a reliability study: review as many components, assemblies, and subsystems as possible to identify **failure modes** (what can fail and how), their **causes**, and their **effects** (the consequences). It is a structured, bottom-up way to surface technical risks before they reach the customer --- and it feeds the same probability--impact thinking used above (in FMEA terms, a **risk priority number** combining severity, occurrence, and detection). ## Key Takeaways - A **risk** is identifiable and can be acted on preemptively; an **uncertainty** cannot. **Risk = Probability × Impact.** Opportunities are the positive mirror. - Four stages: **identify → analyze → mitigate → control & document** (build the knowledge base). - **Qualitative**: plot risks on a **probability--impact matrix**; red-zone risks get a written plan *before* the event. - **Quantitative**: **EMV** = probability × impact; **decision trees** compare choices with chance events; Monte Carlo for whole-network risk. - Responses: **accept, minimize, share, transfer, reserve.** Pick per risk; ring-fence reserve against the biggest ones. - **Task contingency** is the PM's; **managerial contingency** is management's, for the truly unforeseeable. - **FMEA** systematically surfaces technical failure modes, causes, and effects. ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: The road-trip risk register (from the course exercise) Six friends borrow an older car and drive to an unfamiliar beach. The weather forecast is mixed with a chance of rain and high winds; one friend is a very picky eater; the owner plans to replace the car soon due to problems; there is a fireworks show and all-day music at a crowded venue. List the risks, classify each, and give a mitigation strategy. **Model answer (partial).** | Risk | Class | Strategy | |---|---|---| | Get lost / arrive late | Schedule | *Minimize* --- offline map, leave early | | Car breaks down | Technology / Resources | *Minimize* (check oil, tires) + *transfer* (roadside assistance) | | Rain / high winds spoil the day | Weather | *Accept* + *minimize* (pack a tarp, check the radar) | | Picky eater has nothing to eat | Resources | *Minimize* --- bring a known-safe option | | No parking at a crowded venue | Resources | *Minimize* --- arrive before the crowd | | Injury in the crowd / fireworks | Environmental / Safety | *Minimize* --- agree a meeting point, stay together |
Problem 2: EMV of competing suppliers Supplier X: \$140 000, 15 % chance of a 3-week slip costing \$45 000. Supplier Y: \$128 000, 35 % chance of a 3-week slip costing \$45 000. On expected cost alone, which is cheaper? **Solution.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- 140000 + 0.15 * 45000 Y <- 128000 + 0.35 * 45000 cat(sprintf("Supplier X expected cost: $%s\n", format(X, big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("Supplier Y expected cost: $%s\n", format(Y, big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("Cheaper on EMV: Supplier %s\n", ifelse(X < Y, "X", "Y"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Supplier X expected cost: $146 750 Supplier Y expected cost: $143 750 Cheaper on EMV: Supplier Y ``` ::: ::: X: \$146 750. Y: \$143 750. Y is cheaper on expected cost --- but note X's risk is *less likely*, which may matter more than the \$3 000 if a slip would blow the holiday launch window. EMV informs the decision; it does not make it.
Problem 3 (discussion): red-zone risk with no cheap mitigation The "carbon-fibre plant disruption" risk sits in the red zone, but the supplier is the only qualified source and re-qualifying another would take four months you do not have. What are your options? **Discussion points.** You cannot *minimize* the probability much, so work the **impact**: build a larger **contingency reserve** (time and money) against it; **transfer** part of it via contract terms (penalty clauses, guaranteed allocation); **share** it by co-investing in the supplier's modernization for priority supply; carry **safety stock** of the critical carbon-fibre parts; and design a **fallback** (an aluminium body variant) that could be substituted if the supply fails, accepting a heavier product rather than a missed launch.
